Quote (A): In such cases, deployers must employ safeguards to avoid the screening of employees.
Quote (B): In such cases, deployers must employ safeguards to avoid the screening of employees.
Holder (B): deployers of crowd-control, security or medical systems that infer emotions and may also screen staff
Position (A): not stated (deployers of crowd-control or aggression-detection systems, e.g. at stadiums and central stations; public or private)
Note (A): Safeguards are not specified. Applies to out-of-scope systems that may incidentally screen staff (security staff, medical employees). Also coded: Accountability/Design (para 270).
Note (B): Safeguard duty; content of the safeguards not stated. Context: such systems are 'outside the scope of the prohibition' because their 'primary objective' is not employees' emotions. Trigger: ongoing use. Also coded Accountability/Design (deployers 'remain responsible').

Quote (A): Deployers of such systems remain responsible to ensure that employees are not adversely affected by their use.
Quote (B): Deployers of such systems remain responsible to ensure that employees are not adversely affected by their use.
Holder (B): Deployers of such systems (crowd-control, security or medical systems inferring emotions)
Position (A): not stated (deployers, public or private)
Note (A): Named responsibility. To whom the deployer answers: not stated. Consequence: not stated. Also coded: Delivery/Design (para 270).
Note (B): Named responsibility. To whom the deployer answers: not stated; consequence: not stated. On 'ensure': the deployer can stop its own use and must apply the safeguards itself [inference]. Also coded Delivery/Design (same paragraph).

Quote (A): The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities, not to place on the market, put into service or use such AI systems.
Quote (B): The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities, not to place on the market, put into service or use such AI systems.
Holder (B): providers and deployers of AI systems
Position (A): mixed: public authority and outside the state: private companies
Level of obligation (A): statutory duty (prohibition); the Guidelines' reading is non-binding interpretation
If not met (A): not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
Note (A): Prohibition on biometric categorisation of individuals to infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Systems not prohibited are high-risk (para 287, Annex III point 1(b)).
Note (B): Prohibits biometric categorisation systems that 'categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex -life or sexual orientation' (para 271). Five cumulative conditions (para 273). Features 'ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons' fall outside the definition (para 279). Sensitive-attribute categorisation that is not prohibited is classified as high-risk (para 287). The law enforcement labelling exemption is coded separately.

Quote (A): Article 5(1)(g) AI Act also provides that the prohibition in that provision does not apply to the l abelling or filtering of lawfully acquired datasets  in the area of law enforcement
Quote (B): Article 5(1)(g) AI Act also provides that the prohibition in that provision does not apply to the l abelling or filtering of lawfully acquired datasets  in the area of law enforcement.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Statutory (A): statutory: AI Act Art. 5(1)(g) (last phrase) and Recital 30
Note (A): Scope exception. Example: a law enforcement authority labelling and filtering a dataset suspected of containing child sexual abuse material, by gender, age, eye and hair colour, scars, or abusers' hand features, 'is permitted'. Para 285: labelling by protected characteristics may be needed for data quality to prevent discrimination (Arts. 10 and 17 cited).
Note (B): Scope exemption. Example: a law enforcement authority using AI to label and filter a dataset 'suspected of containing child sexual abuse material', including by gender, age, eye and hair colour, scars and markings, to identify victims or suspects 'is permitted'. Para 285: labelling by protected characteristics 'may be necessary for high -quality data, precisely to prevent discrimination', and the AI Act 'may even require labelling operations to conform to the AI Act’s requirements for high-risk AI systems'.

Quote (A): Article 5(1)(h) AI Act  only prohibits the use of real -time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, so that only deployers of such systems are concerned by that provision.
Quote (B): Article 5(1)(h) AI Act  only prohibits the use of real -time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, so that only deployers of such systems are concerned by that provision.
Holder (A): deployers (law enforcement authorities and entities acting on their behalf)
Holder (B): deployers of real-time RBI systems for law enforcement purposes: law enforcement authorities and entities acting on their behalf or entrusted by Member State law
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (and private entities acting on its behalf)
Level of obligation (A): statutory duty (prohibition, subject to exhaustive exceptions)
If not met (A): not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
Note (A): Prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Placing on the market and other RBI uses are not prohibited but are high-risk (Art. 6(2), Annex III point 1(a)); authorised uses also fall under the high-risk rules. Exceptions only under Art. 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) with Art. 5(2)-(7) safeguards (para 289).
Note (B): Only use is prohibited; placing on the market and putting into service are 'subject to the rules for high-risk AI systems' (para 291). Applies 'irrespective of the entity, authority, or body carrying out the law enforcement activities' (para 319). Any use outside the three listed objectives 'is prohibited' (para 328), e.g. police use of real-time RBI 'to identify a shoplifter'. Retrospective (post) RBI is not prohibited but 'subject to additional safeguards' under Art. 26(10) (paras 292, 427). Five cumulative conditions (para 295); the definitional scope readings are coded as separate entries.

Quote (A): In accordance with Article 5(5) AI Act, Member States are free to decide whether and in which of the three situations the use of real-time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is permitted  in their territory.
Quote (B): Member States are free to decide whether and in which of the three situations the use of real-time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is permitted  in their territory
Position (A): public authority: member state
Note (A): Member States decide whether any exception is available nationally. Para 326: Art. 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) is not itself a legal basis; only domestic law meeting Art. 5(2)-(7) can allow use. See the Member-State national-law entries (para 411-418).
Note (B): Allocates the decision whether real-time RBI may be used at all to national law. 'Article 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) AI Act does not in itself constitute a legal basis' (para 326); 'The existence of national legislation that complies with the relevant requirements of the AI Act is therefore a pre-requisite of such use' (para 290). Para 349: 'A Member State may authorise' use to locate and identify suspects. Limits on national law and the option of stricter law are coded under para 413.

Quote (A): AI systems that are intended to be used for biometric verification fall outside the scope of the prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) AI Act
Quote (B): AI systems that are intended to be used for biometric verification fall outside the scope of the prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) AI Act.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (nearest: border authorities, given the example)
Statutory (A): statutory: AI Act Art. 5(1)(h) and Recital 17 (as interpreted)
Note (A): Example: comparing a traveller's face at an e-gate with the passport image. Para 305-306: identity confirmation for access to a service, device or premises is not 'remote'; active involvement requires stepping consciously in front of a camera; being informed of cameras is not enough.
Note (B): Scope exclusion. Example: 'the comparison of a traveller’s face scanned at an e-gate with the facial image contained in their passport'. Para 305: confirming identity for access to a service, device or premises is not 'remote'. Para 306: for active involvement 'it is not sufficient that persons are informed about the presence of cameras'; metro surveillance cameras are remote, biometric metro tickets are not.

Quote (A): In the case of body -cams capable of RBI used by individual law enforcement agents, the untargeted filming during, for example , a demonstration with hundreds of participants will be considered to fulfil the condition of remoteness.
Quote (B): In the case of body -cams capable of RBI used by individual law enforcement agents, the untargeted filming during, for example , a demonstration with hundreds of participants will be considered to fulfil the condition of remoteness.
Holder (B): individual law enforcement agents using RBI-capable body-cams
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Note (A): Brings officer body-cams within the prohibition's remoteness condition. Para 307: voice, gait and keystroke systems may also be RBI, though being an example 'does not imply that they are prohibited'.
Note (B): Brings officer-worn tools within the 'remoteness' condition. Whether a given use is prohibited also depends on real-time use, a publicly accessible space and a law enforcement purpose.

Quote (A): prisons and border control are not publicly accessible spaces
Quote (B): prisons and border control are not publicly accessible spaces
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (nearest: prison and border authorities)
Statutory (A): statutory: AI Act Arts. 3(44), 5(1)(h) and Recital 19 (as interpreted)
Note (A): Scope exclusions: online spaces; workplaces with entry control; prisons; border control. Para 316-317: a border crossing point is excluded but the street leading to it normally is not; airport common areas are publicly accessible, the border-control area is not. Para 314: offices of municipal civil servants may be non-public. Para 318: assessed case by case.
Note (B): Scope exclusion taking prisons and border control out of Art. 5(1)(h). 'a border crossing point is not a publicly accessible space, while the street leading to the border crossing point' normally is (para 316); airport common areas are publicly accessible but the border-control area is excluded (para 317). Online spaces and badge-controlled workplaces are also excluded (para 315); ownership is irrelevant (p. 102 [printed 97]). Accessibility is assessed 'based on a case-by-case analysis' (para 318).

Quote (A): In both cases, the law enforcement authorities must instruct on all major aspects and supervise the other entity, as this requirement is inherent to the notion of acting ‘on behalf’ of a person.
Quote (B): In both cases, the law enforcement authorities must instruct on all major aspects and supervise the other entity, as this requirement is inherent to the notion of acting ‘on behalf’ of a person.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Level of obligation (A): mandatory ('must'); non-binding interpretation of a definition
Note (A): Authority to direct and supervise delegated or requested entities. Also coded: Coordination/Design (delegation, para 324).
Note (B): Authority over delegated use. Examples: public transport companies, sports federations and banks acting 'under their instructions and supervision'. Para 325: only bodies 'entrusted with a specific law enforcement task' fall under 'law enforcement'. Example (p. 133 [printed 128]): a shopping mall 'Entrusted by the police' using real-time RBI to find shoplifters is prohibited. Also coded Coordination/Design (delegation link).

Quote (A): ‘On behalf of’ means that a law enforcement authority has delegated the performance of a law enforcement activity (or part of it) to another entity or person, including private parties
Quote (B): ‘On behalf of’ means that a law enforcement authority has delegated the performance of a law enforcement activity (or part of it) to another entity or person, including private parties
Holder (A): law enforcement authorities; entities or persons acting on their behalf, including private parties
Holder (B): law enforcement authorities (delegating); other entities or persons, including private parties (acting on their behalf)
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority; outside the state: private companies and other bodies
Note (A): Delegation or case-specific request linking a law enforcement authority with another body. Examples: public transport companies, sports federations, banks acting under police instructions and supervision. Entities acting 'on their own behalf' (e.g. against fraud) are not covered. Also coded: Decision-making/Design (instruct and supervise).
Note (B): Delegation, or a case-by-case request, as the formal link between law enforcement and other bodies; such bodies then fall within 'law enforcement'. Prior authorisation is needed 'even if the systems are operated by other parties  on behalf of law enforcement authorities , for example sport clubs or shopping malls' (para 386). Also coded Decision-making/Design (instruct and supervise).

Quote (A): the use of real-time RBI systems to search for that person would not be deemed to be for law enforcement purposes and  would therefore fall under the rules for such use under the GDPR.
Quote (B): the use of real-time RBI systems to search for that person would not be deemed to be for law enforcement purposes and  would therefore fall under the rules for such use under the GDPR.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (nearest: authorities searching for missing persons)
Note (A): Searches for a vulnerable missing person under an administrative procedure, with no suspicion of crime, fall outside the prohibition (GDPR applies instead). Para 334: Art. 5(1)(h)(i) only allows missing-person searches for law enforcement purposes.
Note (B): Scope: the same public search falls in or out of the prohibition depending on whether it is for law enforcement purposes; Art. 5(1)(h)(i) 'only allows the use of a real-time RBI system to search for missing persons for law enforcement purposes' (para 334). Related examples (p. 121 [printed 116], para 386): a non-law-enforcement organisation searching for missing children is outside the prohibition but high-risk, and 'prior consultation of the su pervisory data protection authority may be necessary pursuant to Article 36 GDPR'.

Quote (A): The police are not allowed to deploy real-time facial recognition technologies  in a broad, untargeted manner, i.e. in the hope of finding wanted criminal s and taking them off the streets.
Quote (B): The police are not allowed to deploy real-time facial recognition technologies  in a broad, untargeted manner, i.e. in the hope of finding wanted criminal s and taking them off the streets.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Statutory (A): statutory: AI Act Art. 5(1)(h)(iii) and Annex II (as interpreted)
Note (A): Festival example. Offences must be in the Annex II list and punishable by a maximum of at least four years (para 351, 354); a European Arrest Warrant is not required (para 353). A targeted search for a named suspect believed to be present 'may be covered'.
Note (B): Hypothetical example, coded as design. Same reading elsewhere: law enforcement authorities 'are prohibited from using  real-time facial recognition systems in the street based on general security, crime prevention and over-crowding concerns' (p. 113 [printed 108], para 359 example); a stadium watchlist 'is too unspecific and is not linked to the event of the football match.  Such use would therefore be prohibited' (p. 131 [printed 126], s. 10.8); city cameras at places of worship, LGBT+ venues and doctors' offices: 'the unspecified and indiscriminate identification of natural persons, is prohibited' (p. 132 [printed 127]). Contrast: a targeted search for a named suspect under a European Arrest Warrant 'may be covered'; tracking a terror-attack offender 'can be permitted' (p. 111 [printed 106]).

Quote (A): the deployment of a real-time RBI system in publicly accessible spaces  for law enforcement purposes  should only be authorized for targeted individuals.
Quote (B): the deployment of a real-time RBI system in publicly accessible spaces  for law enforcement purposes  should only be authorized for targeted individuals.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (nearest: authorising authorities and law enforcement deployers)
Level of obligation (A): statutory condition ('only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual'); Guidelines' reading non-binding
Note (A): Targeting condition. Para 358: use may only start to search for specific individuals the authorities have reason to believe are victims or involved in a listed scenario; for (ii) and (iii) the identity need not be known if a reference database of the group has been constituted.
Note (B): Limits who may be searched for, 'to avoid mass surveillance' (para 357). Use 'may only be initiated to search for specific individuals for which the law enforcement authorities have reasons to believe or are informed' that they are victims or involved in a listed scenario (para 358). For scenarios (ii) and (iii) the identity need not be known beforehand, 'provided the law enforcement authorities have  constituted a reference database' of the group (para 358).

Quote (A): before deployment, the law enforcement authority deploying the real-time RBI system must have conducted a Fundamental Right Impact Assessment (FRIA) and registered the system in the EU database (except in a duly justified case).
Quote (B): before deployment, the law enforcement authority deploying the real-time RBI system must have conducted a Fundamental Right Impact Assessment (FRIA) and registered the system in the EU database (except in a duly justified case).
Holder (A): the law enforcement authority deploying the real-time RBI system
Holder (B): the law enforcement authority deploying the real-time RBI system (deployer); not entities acting on its behalf (para 373)
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
If not met (A): use may not be authorised: Art. 5(2) as quoted, 'shall be authorised only if the law enforcement authority has completed a  fundamental rights impact assessment'
Note (A): Impact assessment before deployment (para 374). Para 373: the duty rests on the deployer, not on bodies acting on its behalf. Para 371: 'A FRIA is an accountability tool'; to whom it is answered is not stated. Para 372: complements the DPIA without overlap. Registration is coded separately as Accountability/Design (para 377).
Note (B): Impact assessment. Trigger: 'before the deployment' (para 374), 'at an abstract level, prior to the first putting into service' (p. 117 [printed 112]); each individual use is then authorised separately. Must comply with Art. 27 (para 369). Interim reading: before high-risk rules apply (2 August 2026), 'the requirements for FRIA set out in Article 27 AI Act should be implemented by the deployers' of real-time RBI (para 370). The document calls the FRIA 'an accountability tool' (para 371); to whom its results go is not stated in this part. FRIA content coded in separate entries; registration coded as Accountability/Design (para 377).

Quote (A): is aimed to serve as a preliminary guidance for deployers in this interim period before the AI Office provides a template.
Quote (B): is aimed to serve as a preliminary guidance for deployers in this interim period before the AI Office provides a template.
Holder (A): European Commission (these Guidelines); AI Office (template, forthcoming)
Position (A): public authority: EU institution
Statutory (A): non-statutory: Commission Guidelines (interim guidance); template under AI Act Art. 27 (not yet provided)
Note (A): Resource: the FRIA guidance in para 375-376 is an official offer; the AI Office template is promised, not yet provided (para 370 also says the Commission will provide 'further guidance on the obligation under Article 27'). Serves the FRIA entries (Delivery/Design, para 368, 370, 375).
Note (B): Provided resource serving the FRIA (Delivery/Design). Status: preliminary guidance is given in these guidelines; the template is future, applying 'before the obligations for high-risk AI systems become applicable and the Commission adopts the template for FRIA' and gives 'further guidance on the obligation under Article 27' (para 370). Scope limited to authorised real-time RBI: 'the analysis does not cover the case of high-risk AI systems in general' (fn 214).

Quote (A): If other actors are acting on behalf of the deployer/the law enforcement authority, they will have to contribute to the preparation of the FRIA with all relevant information to ensure it is properly carried out.
Quote (B): If other actors are acting on behalf of the deployer/the law enforcement authority, they will have to contribute to the preparation of the FRIA with all relevant information to ensure it is properly carried out.
Holder (A): other actors acting on behalf of the deployer / the law enforcement authority
Holder (B): other actors acting on behalf of the deployer/the law enforcement authority
Position (A): mixed: public bodies and outside the state: private parties acting on behalf of law enforcement
Note (A): Information flow from delegated actors to the deployer. The FRIA duty itself stays with the deployer.
Note (B): Information flow from delegated operators to the deployer that carries the FRIA duty: 'The obligation to carry out the FRIA under Article 5(2) AI Act  is imposed on the deployers of the RBI system , and not entities or bodies or anyone else acting on their behalf.' Also coded Delivery/Design (FRIA, para 368).

Quote (A): the FRIA must identify the fundamental rights of those persons and assess the impact on their fundamental rights, including the  severity of the impact  and its scale, taking into account the potentially affected persons.
Quote (B): the FRIA must identify the fundamental rights of those persons and assess the impact on their fundamental rights, including the  severity of the impact  and its scale, taking into account the potentially affected persons.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Level of obligation (A): mandatory ('must'); content guidance is non-binding interpretation
Note (A): FRIA content (para 375): description of use (deployer name, law enforcement purposes, reference database and data sources, technology, legal basis); general period and frequency of use; categories of persons (target, persons in the reference database, persons in the area); specific risks. Para 376 lists rights at stake. Trigger: 'at an abstract level, prior to the first putting into service'; case-specific points go into each authorisation request. Should also assess necessity and proportionality, including less intrusive alternatives.
Note (B): Rights listed in para 376 include privacy and 'reasonable expectation of anonymity in public spaces', data protection, expression and assembly (a 'chilling effect'), effective remedy, non-discrimination ('misidentification'), dignity, presumption of innocence, and rights of children and the elderly. The FRIA should also assess 'whether the use of a r eal-time RBI system is necessary and proportionate', including 'less intrusive alternatives'. Trigger: before first putting into service, at an abstract level; case-specific matters go into each authorisation request.

Quote (A): The FRIA should describe the performance and accuracy level of the system, based on the technical documentation and, if available, the training data on which the technology was tested and developed to prevent biases and discrimination.
Quote (B): The FRIA should describe the performance and accuracy level of the system, based on the technical documentation and, if available, the training data on which the technology was tested and developed to prevent biases and discrimination.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Statutory (A): statutory: AI Act Arts. 5(2) and 27 (as interpreted)
Note (A): Check of system performance. Trigger: before first putting into service. Compared against: technical documentation and, if available, training and testing data. Metric: 'performance and accuracy level' named; no threshold given. Provider documentation coded as Delivery/Resources.
Note (B): Check of system performance. Trigger: within the FRIA, before first putting into service. Compared against: the provider's technical documentation and, if available, the training data. Metric: 'performance and accuracy level'; no threshold stated. Related: national law may require 'the minimum reliability, threshold used, and accuracy rates' in authorisation requests (p. 128 [printed 123]; separate entry).

Quote (A): the description of the technology underlying the system to explain its functioning (by referencing the available documentation provided by the provider and its name)
Quote (B): the description of the technology underlying the system to explain its functioning (by referencing the available documentation provided by the provider and its name)
Holder (B): the provider of the RBI system
Position (A): outside the state: private companies (providers) [inference: providers are usually private]
Note (A): Information from the provider that the deployer uses in the FRIA. Fn 215: once high-risk rules apply, this can be done by reference to the system's EU database registration number. Serves the FRIA entries (Delivery/Design, para 375).
Note (B): Information resource from the provider, used by the deployer in the FRIA. The FRIA's accuracy description is also 'based on the technical documentation and, if available, the training data' (p. 117 [printed 112]). Fn 215: once high-risk rules apply, reference can be made to 'the registration number of the system in the EU database'. Whether the provider must supply the documentation is not stated in this passage.

Quote (A): The person in charge of human oversight should have sufficient ‘AI literacy, training and auth ority’216 to understand how the system functions and when it underperforms or malfunctions.
Quote (B): The person in charge of human oversight should have sufficient ‘AI literacy, training and auth ority’216 to understand how the system functions and when it underperforms or malfunctions.
Location (A): page 117 (printed p. 112), section 10.1.1, para 375 (human oversight measures)
Holder (A): the person in charge of human oversight
Holder (B): the deployer (the person in charge of human oversight)
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (staff of law enforcement deployers)
Statutory (A): statutory: AI Act Arts. 4 and 14; Recital 91 (as cited)
Note (A): Skills, training and authority for the overseer; who provides them is not stated (nearest: deployer). Serves the human-oversight entries (para 375, 407).
Note (B): Skills, training and authority required of the holder, not provided by a named actor ('216' in the quote is a footnote marker). Serves the human-oversight procedures entry (same page). The procedures should also 'provide training to operate the system'.

Quote (A): the deployer should explain redress measures in case a risk materialises , including the governance procedures and the complaint mechanisms (such as in  the case of a misidentification).
Quote (B): the deployer should explain redress measures in case a risk materialises , including the governance procedures and the complaint mechanisms (such as in  the case of a misidentification).
Location (A): page 118 (printed p. 113), section 10.1.1, para 375 (risk mitigation measures)
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Note (A): Redress and complaint routes to be described in the FRIA. To whom the deployer answers: not stated (affected persons, e.g. those misidentified [inference]). Consequence: not stated.
Note (B): Redress and complaint routes for affected persons, e.g. after misidentification. To whom: affected persons through complaint mechanisms [inference]; consequence: not stated. The deployer is asked to 'explain' its measures in the FRIA; no specific mechanism is required.

Quote (A): Article 5(2) AI Act also obliges the deployer of a real-time RBI system used in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes  to register  the system in the EU database provided  for in Article 49 AI Act .
Quote (B): Article 5(2) AI Act also obliges the deployer of a real-time RBI system used in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes  to register  the system in the EU database provided  for in Article 49 AI Act
Holder (A): the deployer of a real-time RBI system (law enforcement authority)
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
If not met (A): use may not be authorised without registration (Art. 5(2) as quoted), except in duly justified urgency with registration 'without undue delay'
Note (A): Registration. 'Undue delay' means 'as soon as possible', case by case, not caused by deliberate action; example: registration within 24 hours after a live-shooter deployment 'might be considered a reasonable delay'. Registration is in a non-public section (Coordination/Resources entry, para 377), so this is not publication.
Note (B): Registration. Urgency: 'deployment may start even prior to registration, provided the law enforcement authority registers the system without undue delay'; 'The delay should not be caused by a deliberate action'; example: registration 'within 24 hours of the use might be considered a reasonable delay' (live shooter). Publication is limited: registration is in a 'non -public section' (Coordination entry). To whom the deployer answers: not stated.

Quote (A): must be authorized by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority prior to its use. This is the main principle.
Quote (B): must be authorized by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority prior to its use. This is the main principle.
Holder (A): a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, of the Member State where the use takes place
Holder (B): judicial authority or independent administrative authority of the Member State, whose decision is binding
Position (A): public authority: member-state judicial or independent administrative authority
If not met (A): use is prohibited; in urgency, if authorisation is rejected 'the use shall be stopped with immediate effect' and all data and outputs deleted (Art. 5(3) as quoted)
Note (A): Prior authorisation of 'each use' (para 387), not of installation: police installing biometric-ready CCTV at a station need no authorisation, but need a FRIA before first use and authorisation before each use. Applies also when systems are operated by others on behalf of law enforcement, e.g. sport clubs or shopping malls (para 386). Art. 5(3): grant 'only where it is satisfied, on the basis of objective evidence or clear indications'. Check coded as Delivery/Design (para 380).
Note (B): Approval gate for each use: 'the decisive moment for obtaining such authorisation is not the  moment prior to installing real-time RBI systems, but each concrete use thereof' (para 387). Needed 'even if the systems are operated by other parties  on behalf of law enforcement authorities' (para 386). 'The authorisation may only be granted by a judicial or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding' (para 390). Granted only where the authority 'is satisfied, on the basis of objective evidence or clear indications presented to it' of necessity and proportionality (Art. 5(3) as quoted, p. 119 [printed 114]). Urgency exception coded separately. Also coded Delivery/Design (the authority's necessity assessment).

Quote (A): Article 5(3) AI Act requires each individual request for the use of real-time RBI to be ‘reasoned’ and hence substantiated and motivated.
Quote (B): Article 5(3) AI Act requires each individual request for the use of real-time RBI to be ‘reasoned’ and hence substantiated and motivated.
Holder (A): the deployer, i.e. the competent (law enforcement) authority
Holder (B): the deployer, i.e. the competent (law enforcement) authority (para 384: 'it may be assumed')
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority
Note (A): The deployer answers to the authorising authority. Para 384: who requests is not specified in the Act; the Guidelines assume the deployer, including bodies entrusted under Art. 3(45)(b). Para 389: national law should set the exact content of the request, including evidence of strict necessity and proportionality. Para 394: the request goes to the authority competent under national law. Also a coordination link (request procedure).
Note (B): Answers to: the authorising judicial or independent administrative authority. Para 384: 'Whilst not specified, it may be assumed that the request will normally be initiated by the deployer'. Para 389: national legislation 'should lay down requirements regarding the exact content of the request', including 'sufficient evidence to determine the strict necessity and proportionality'. In urgency the request 'should motivate why no prior request was submitted' (para 401).

Quote (A): implying that the authorising authority needs to be independent from the authority using the RBI system.
Quote (B): implying that the authorising authority needs to be independent from the authority using the RBI system.
Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (nearest: Member States designating the authorising authority)
Note (A): Standard for who decides. Applies to the police and to investigative judges or prosecutors who supervise the police's use. Para 392: independence means acting 'completely freely', 'shielded from any instructions or pressure' (CJEU). Para 393: judicial authorities are in general independent. Para 390: the decision must be binding.
Note (B): Who may decide. Independence 'would apply not only for the police, but also cases of investigative judges or prosecutors that supervise the work of police'; a prosecutor involved in the investigation lacks independence (Prokuratuur). Independence means being 'shielded from any instructions or pressure' (para 392). The request goes to 'the authority that is competent according to national law' (para 394).

Quote (A): if an authorisation request  in the case of urgency is rejected, the use of the real -time RBI system should be ceased with immediate effect.

Position (A): public authority: member-state authority (independent data protection supervisory authority)
Statutory (A): non-statutory: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 (Art. 64(2) GDPR), interpreting GDPR Art. 4(1) and Recital 26
Level of obligation (A): non-binding interpretation addressed to SAs, which 'should take utmost account' of the Opinion (para 15); verb 'should'
Note (A): Verb 'should'. Authority over scope: whether a model trained on personal data falls outside the GDPR as anonymous is decided by the SA case by case (para 34: 'the determination of whether an AI model is anonymous should be assessed, based on specific criteria, on a case-by-case basis'; executive summary names 'competent SAs'). Evidence must show, with reasonable means, (i) personal data related to the training data cannot be extracted and (ii) outputs do not relate to training-data subjects. Trigger: a controller's claim of anonymity. Compared against: likelihood of extraction or of obtaining personal data via queries, to be 'insignificant' (para 43); no quantified metric. Para 43: 'By default, SAs should consider that  AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood  of identification'. Para 134: 'a mere assertion of anonymity of the model is not enough to exempt it from the application of the GDPR'. EDPB standard coded separately (Decision-making/Design, para 43); controller's answerability coded Accountability/Design (paras 45, 57).
Note (B): Verb 'should'. The SA decides whether to accept a controller's claim that a model is anonymous, which decides whether the GDPR applies to its later operation (para 134). Trigger: a controller's claim of anonymity. Compares against: (i) personal data related to the training data cannot be extracted and (ii) outputs do not relate to training-data subjects, with reasonable means. Metric: likelihood must be 'insignificant' (para 43); not quantified. Also coded Delivery/Design (para 45, SA evaluation of measures).

'37' is a footnote marker in the extraction. The Opinion is advisory, so this could alternatively be read as Resources (guidance to SAs); coded Decision-making because it sets the standard. Applied by SAs (Decision-making/Design, para 38).
Note (B): Standard set by the EDPB for when an AI model counts as anonymous: both (i) the likelihood of direct (including probabilistic) extraction of training personal data and (ii) the likelihood of obtaining it from queries should be insignificant, taking into account 'all the means reasonably likely to be used' and unintended (re)use or disclosure. '37' is a footnote marker. Default: 'SAs should consider that AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood of identification' (para 43). Models designed to provide personal data of training subjects 'cannot be considered anonymous' (para 29). Whoever sets a standard is decision-making; SAs apply it (see para 38 entry).
